claim: The human visual system can be divided into over two-dozen distinct areas, each containing a topographic map of the visual field.
source: The human visual system can be divided into over two-dozen distinct areas, each of which contains a topographic map of the visual field.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review literature on visual mapping studies.

claim: The correlation pattern between visual areas reflected the underlying receptive field organization with higher correlations between cortical sites containing overlapping representations of visual space.
source: The correlation pattern between areas reflected the underlying receptive field organization with higher correlations between cortical sites containing overlapping representations of visual space.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The correlation pattern reflected the underlying widespread eccentricity organization of visual cortex, with highest correlations observed for cortical sites with iso-eccentricity representations including regions with non-overlapping representations of visual space.
source: In addition, the correlation pattern reflected the underlying widespread eccentricity organization of visual cortex, in which the highest correlations were observed for cortical sites with iso-eccentricity representations including regions with non-overlapping representations of visual space.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The eccentricity-based correlation pattern appears to be part of an intrinsic functional architecture that supports the integration of information across functionally specialized visual areas.
source: This eccentricity-based correlation pattern appears to be part of an intrinsic functional architecture that supports the integration of information across functionally specialized visual areas.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data findings, involving inference about functional significance.

claim: Early electrophysiological recordings in monkeys and cats identified several representations of the contralateral visual field in and around the calcarine sulcus.
source: Early electrophysiological recordings in monkeys and cats identified several representations of the contralateral visual field in and around the calcarine sulcus (Daniel and Whitteridge, 1961; Zeki, 1969; Allman and Kaas, 1971; Van Essen et al., 1984).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior electrophysiological studies.

claim: Through the use of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), the human visual system contains over two-dozen visual maps.
source: Through the use of functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), it has now become evident that the human visual system contains over two-dozen visual maps (for review of original mapping studies, see Silver and Kastner, 2009; Wandell and Winawer, 2011; Abdollahi et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to review literature.

claim: The topographic organization of individual areas is thought to provide an infrastructure for the integration of information across areas and along the visual hierarchy.
source: The topographic organization of individual areas is thought to provide an infrastructure for the integration of information across areas and along the visual hierarchy (Kaas, 1997; Wandell et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: Anatomical studies in primates have demonstrated that neurons with overlapping receptive fields (RFs) are interconnected.
source: Anatomical studies in primates have demonstrated that neurons with overlapping receptive fields (RFs) are interconnected (Cragg, 1969; Zeki, 1969; Van Essen and Zeki, 1978; Maunsell and Van Essen, 1983).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: fMRI connectivity studies in humans have demonstrated topographically-local correlations between regions with overlapping visual field representations.
source: Similarly, fMRI connectivity studies in humans have demonstrated topographically-local correlations between regions with overlapping visual field representations (Heinzle et al., 2011; Haak et al., 2012; Butt et al., 2013; Donner et al., 2013; Gravel et al., 2014; Raemaekers et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior fMRI studies.

claim: Widespread functional correlation patterns have been observed across visual cortex in macaques and humans.
source: In addition, widespread functional correlation patterns have been observed across visual cortex in macaques (Leopold et al., 2003; Vincent et al., 2007) and humans (Nir et al., 2006, 2008; Yeo et al., 2011; Donner et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior studies in both species.

claim: Widespread correlation patterns contain broad differences between foveal and peripheral cortex.
source: These patterns contain broad differences between foveal and peripheral cortex (Raemaekers et al., 2014), though may also be tied to the fine-scale organization of individual retinotopic maps.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to a prior study, with speculation about additional organization.

claim: Correlation patterns were consistent across subjects and experiments.
source: Correlation patterns were consistent across subjects and experiments.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: The widespread correlation pattern based on eccentricity representation was observed between upper and lower visual field representations, within and across visual areas, and between hemispheres.
source: This eccentricity-based correlation pattern was observed between upper and lower visual field representations, within and across visual areas, and between hemispheres.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's data analysis.

claim: Correlation patterns were similar in the presence and absence of bottom-up visual input.
source: Moreover, correlation patterns were similar in the presence and absence of bottom-up visual input.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing different experimental conditions.

claim: The measured correlation pattern could not be accounted for by overlapping RFs, inter-hemisphere homotopic connections, anatomical distance, eye movements, subject motion, or physiological noise.
source: Finally, the measured correlation pattern could not be accounted for by overlapping RFs, inter-hemisphere homotopic connections, anatomical distance, eye movements, subject motion, or physiological noise.
evidence: This is a conclusion from control analyses performed in the study.

claim: The widespread pattern is part of an intrinsic functional architecture of the visual system that could reflect eccentricity-dependent processing.
source: We propose that this widespread pattern is part of an intrinsic functional architecture of the visual system that could reflect eccentricity-dependent processing.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Retinotopy and correlation patterns were characterized and compared within the visual systems of 14 participants.
source: Retinotopy and correlation patterns were characterized and compared within the visual systems of 14 participants.
evidence: This describes the study design and sample size.

claim: Retinotopic organization of the visual system was examined within the central 15° of visual space using a conventional travelling wave paradigm.
source: Retinotopic organization of the visual system was examined within the central 15° of visual space using a conventional travelling wave paradigm in which eccentricity and polar angle maps were collected to define visual areas V1, V2, V3, V3A–B, hV4, VO1–2 (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This describes the experimental methods used.

claim: For any individual node, correlation coefficients with all other nodes within visual cortex typically ranged between −0.10 and 0.75 in individual subjects after cerebrospinal fluid and white matter signal regression.
source: For any individual node, correlation coefficients with all other nodes within visual cortex typically ranged between −0.10 and 0.75 in individual subjects (after cerebrospinal fluid and white matter signal regression).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Each of the four seed locations was strongly correlated with adjacent cortex.
source: Each of the four seed locations was strongly correlated (red / yellow) with adjacent cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from the seed-based correlation analysis, with reference to figure colors.

claim: The strongest correlations with each seed extended across visual cortex and spanned several visual areas, from V1 to V3A–B, dorsally, and to VO1–2 ventrally.
source: In addition, the strongest correlations with each seed extended across visual cortex and spanned several visual areas, from V1 to V3A–B, dorsally, and to VO1–2 ventrally.
evidence: This is a finding from the seed-based correlation analysis.

claim: Strong correlations with nodes adjacent to the seed and within ipsilateral dorsal cortex likely reflect well-established connectivity based on overlapping visual field representations.
source: Strong correlations with nodes adjacent to the seed and within ipsilateral dorsal cortex likely reflect well-established connectivity based on overlapping visual field representations (see Heinzle et al., 2011; Haak et al., 2012; Butt et al., 2013), but may also reflect the intrinsic spatial spread of the BOLD signal (Engel et al., 1997; Parkes et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings supported by citations, with acknowledgment of potential confounds.

claim: Despite anatomical distance and representing a different part of visual space, the eccentricity representation of peak correlations within ventral occipital cortex corresponded to that of the seed location.
source: Despite anatomical distance and representing a different part of visual space, the eccentricity representation (distance from fovea) of peak correlations within ventral occipital cortex corresponded to that of the seed location.
evidence: This is a finding from the seed-based correlation analysis.

claim: Local and widespread correlation patterns were observed in most individual subjects and the group average data for dorsal and ventral cortex seeds in V2 and V3, regardless of seeding near the horizontal or vertical meridians.
source: Local and widespread correlation patterns were observed in most individual subjects and the group average data for dorsal and ventral cortex seeds in V2 and V3, regardless of seeding near the horizontal or vertical meridians (see Figure 1—figure supplements 1, 2 for additional individual subject data).
evidence: This is a finding from the seed-based correlation analysis across subjects.

claim: The BOLD signals in areas with eccentricity preferences similar to the seed were correlated in the presence and absence of visual input, even in cases where the spatial receptive fields (RFs) were non-overlapping.
source: The BOLD signals in areas with eccentricity preferences similar to the seed were correlated in the presence and absence of visual input, even in cases where the spatial receptive fields (RFs) were non-overlapping (i.e., across lower and upper or right and left visual field representations).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing different experimental conditions.

claim: Peak correlations were evident in parts of the visual field around each seed location with strong correlations also extending across the visual field along an eccentricity ring corresponding to that of the seed location.
source: Peak correlations (red) were evident in parts of the visual field around each seed location with strong correlations (red / yellow) also extending across the visual field along an eccentricity ring corresponding to that of the seed location.
evidence: This is a finding from the visual field projection analysis, with reference to figure colors.

claim: Similar local and widespread eccentricity-based correlation patterns were observed in data from the movie viewing experiment.
source: Similar local and widespread eccentricity-based correlation patterns were observed in data from the movie viewing experiment (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the movie viewing condition, with reference to a figure.

claim: Individual subject and group average correlation patterns were similar to previously reported group average correlation patterns.
source: Individual subject and group average correlation patterns were similar to previously reported group average correlation patterns (Yeo et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior literature supported by citation.

claim: Correlations between dorsal and ventral bins of V1, V2, and V3 were strongest for iso-eccentricity representations.
source: Correlations between dorsal and ventral bins of V1, V2, and V3 were strongest for iso-eccentricity representations.
evidence: This is a finding from the eccentricity binning analysis.

claim: These correlations were seen across the vertical and horizontal meridians at both foveal and peripheral-most bins.
source: These correlations were seen across the vertical and horizontal meridians at both foveal and peripheral-most bins.
evidence: This is a finding from the eccentricity binning analysis.

claim: For each of the selected dorsal V3 bins, correlations with ventral V3 bins were strongest at (and around) corresponding iso-eccentricities.
source: For each of the selected dorsal V3 bins, correlations with ventral V3 bins were strongest at (and around) corresponding iso-eccentricities (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from the eccentricity binning analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The entire correlation matrix for all eccentricity locations between dorsal and ventral V3 revealed a pattern where correlations were strongest among ventral and dorsal bins with iso-eccentricity representations (i.e., the diagonal), and were weaker for bins with large radial distances.
source: The entire correlation matrix for all eccentricity locations between dorsal and ventral V3 (Figure 4C, center panel), revealed a similar pattern, where correlations were strongest among ventral and dorsal bins with iso-eccentricity representations (i.e., the diagonal), and were weaker for bins with large radial distances (e.g., foveal vs peripheral-most).
evidence: This is a finding from the eccentricity binning analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The group average bin data was strongly correlated with the predicted eccentricity pattern (r = 0.84) and was not positively correlated with cortical distance (r = −0.04) or volume distance (r = −0.19).
source: Indeed, the group average bin data was strongly correlated with the predicted eccentricity pattern (r = 0.84) and was not positively correlated with cortical distance (r = −0.04) or volume distance (r = −0.19) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the correlation analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Individual subject matrices were also correlated with radial distance (mean r = 0.45), and the Fisher-transformed correlations significantly differed from zero across subjects (one-sample t-test, t(13) = 6.37, p < 0.0001).
source: Individual subject matrices were also correlated with radial distance (mean r = 0.45), and the Fisher-transformed correlations significantly differed from zero across subjects (one-sample t-test, t(13) = 6.37, p < 0.0001).
evidence: This is a quantitative statistical finding from the individual subject analysis.

claim: For all comparisons in each condition the strongest correlations were consistently between bins at comparable eccentricity locations (i.e., along the diagonal of each sub-matrix in Figure 5).
source: For all comparisons in each condition the strongest correlations (red/yellow) were consistently between bins at comparable eccentricity locations (i.e., along the diagonal of each sub-matrix in Figure 5).
evidence: This is a finding from the comprehensive area comparison analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: This was the case even for correlations between dorsal and ventral visual portions of V1, V2, and V3, and between hemispheres, which represent mostly discrete parts of visual space.
source: This was the case even for correlations between dorsal and ventral visual portions of V1, V2, and V3, and between hemispheres, which represent mostly discrete parts of visual space.
evidence: This is a finding emphasizing the robustness of the eccentricity effect.

claim: Across area pairs, the average individual subject correlation coefficient with radial distance ranged between 0.17 and 0.80 with a median of 0.39 and an interquartile range of 0.12.
source: Across area pairs, the average individual subject correlation coefficient with radial distance ranged between 0.17 and 0.80 with a median of 0.39 and an interquartile range of 0.12.
evidence: This is a quantitative summary of the correlation analysis across area pairs.

claim: Fisher-transformed individual subject correlations significantly differed from zero for all pairs in each experiment except for two pairs of inter-hemisphere correlations with hV4 in the movie viewing condition.
source: Fisher-transformed individual subject correlations significantly differed from zero for all pairs in each experiment (one-sample t-test, t(13) > 2.31, ps < 0.05, FDR-corrected) except for two pairs of inter-hemisphere correlations with hV4 in the movie viewing condition (ps = 0.13 and 0.07).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis.

claim: In all experiments, individual subject correlations with radial distance were generally strongest for early visual areas (V1, V2, and V3).
source: In all experiments, individual subject correlations with radial distance were generally strongest for early visual areas (V1, V2, and V3).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing correlation strengths across areas.

claim: This could reflect the relatively smaller, more spatially focal receptive fields in early visual areas, but also the larger surface area (i.e., more data points).
source: This could reflect the relatively smaller, more spatially focal receptive fields in early visual areas, but also the larger surface area (i.e., more data points).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the finding.

claim: For each area pair, correlation coefficients were positive at 0–radial distance, and decreased at larger radial distances across the visual field.
source: For each area pair, correlation coefficients were positive at 0–radial distance, and decreased at larger radial distances across the visual field.
evidence: This is a finding from the radial distance analysis.

claim: Iso-eccentricity bins were positively correlated, regardless of visual field quadrant.
source: As illustrated by resting state correlations within and between areas V2 and V3 (Figure 6A), iso-eccentricity bins were positively correlated, regardless of visual field quadrant.
evidence: This is a finding from the radial distance analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: This was observed in all experiment conditions and area comparisons, and individual subject Fisher-transformed correlations significantly differed from zero (ps < 0.05, FDR corrected).
source: This was observed in all experiment conditions and area comparisons, and individual subject Fisher-transformed correlations significantly differed from zero (ps < 0.05, FDR corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis.

claim: Correlation coefficients decreased at larger radial distances for foveal and peripheral-most bins in each quadrant, regardless of magnitude difference.
source: Correlation coefficients decreased at larger radial distances for foveal and peripheral-most bins in each quadrant, regardless of this magnitude difference (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from the radial distance analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The relative decrease in correlation strength as a function of radial distance was similar across the visual field and across experiments.
source: The relative decrease in correlation strength as a function of radial distance was similar across the visual field and across experiments (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a finding from the radial distance analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Correlations between dorsal and ventral portions of V2 and V3 were strongest at 0–radial distance, and steadily decreased at larger radial distances for all conditions.
source: Consistent with the radial arc plots (Figure 6A), correlations between dorsal and ventral portions of V2 and V3 were strongest at 0–radial distance, and steadily decreased at larger radial distances for all conditions (Figure 6; top row).
evidence: This is a finding from the radial distance analysis, with reference to figures.

claim: Similar correlation patterns as a function of radial bin distance were observed across hemispheres, both along the horizontal plane and diagonally across the upper and lower visual fields.
source: We observed similar correlation patterns as a function of radial bin distance across hemispheres, both along the horizontal plane (e.g., RH V2v and LH V2v; middle row) and diagonally across the upper and lower visual fields (e.g., RH V2v and LH V2d; bottom row).
evidence: This is a finding from the radial distance analysis.

claim: The patterns were observed even after removal of horizontal and vertical meridian data, further demonstrating that these effects are unlikely to be driven by local, overlapping visual field representations.
source: The patterns were observed even after removal of horizontal and vertical meridian data, further demonstrating that these effects are unlikely to be driven by local, overlapping visual field representations (Box 1; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from a control analysis, with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: The decrease in correlation coefficients at larger radial bin distances yielded negative slopes from linear fits in each subject for all V2 and V3 pairs.
source: The decrease in correlation coefficients at larger radial bin distances yielded negative slopes from linear fits in each subject for all V2 and V3 pairs.
evidence: This is a finding from the linear regression analysis.

claim: For any given pair, negative slopes were similar across condition.
source: For any given pair, negative slopes were similar across condition.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing slopes across conditions.

claim: Across V2 and V3 pairs, the average individual subject slope of the linear fit ranged between −0.22 and −0.49.
source: Across V2 and V3 pairs, the average individual subject slope of the linear fit ranged between −0.22 and −0.49.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the linear regression analysis.

claim: The average individual subject slope for each area pair was greater than 97.5% of a permuted distribution where the labels of radial distances were scrambled.
source: Further, the average individual subject slope for each area pair was greater than 97.5% of a permuted distribution (mean 97.5% across areas, conditions = −0.06) where the labels of radial distances were scrambled before deriving individual subject radial distance correlations and slopes.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the permutation test.

claim: The slopes were similar across regional comparisons, though were slightly shallower for comparisons that spanned both quadrants and hemispheres.
source: As seen in the radial plots (Figure 6B), the slopes were similar across regional comparisons, though were slightly shallower for comparisons that spanned both quadrants and hemispheres (i.e., diagonal; bottom row).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing slopes across different types of comparisons, with reference to a figure.

claim: These effects were observed during resting fixation and eyes closed conditions, as well as during the processing of the movie, attesting to the robustness of the effect, and excluding many potential confounds.
source: Finally, we observed these effects during resting fixation and eyes closed conditions, as well as during the processing of the movie, attesting to the robustness of the effect, and excluding many potential confounds (see 'Control analyses').
evidence: This is a finding from comparing across experimental conditions.

claim: The magnitude of correlation coefficients linearly decreased as a function of radial bin distance for all area comparisons (V1, V2, V3, hV4, VO1–2, V3A–B), though slopes were generally steeper for comparisons between V1, V2, and V3.
source: The magnitude of correlation coefficients linearly decreased as a function of radial bin distance for all area comparisons (V1, V2, V3, hV4, VO1–2, V3A–B), though slopes were generally steeper for comparisons between V1, V2, and V3.
evidence: This is a finding from the comprehensive area comparison analysis.

claim: Across all areas, average individual subject slopes ranged between −0.14 and −0.80, and each was greater than 97.5% of the permuted distribution.
source: Across all areas, average individual subject slopes ranged between −0.14 and −0.80, and each was greater than 97.5% of the permuted distribution (mean 97.5% across areas, conditions = −0.09).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the comprehensive analysis with permutation testing.

claim: For comparisons between dorsal areas, between ventral areas, and between mirror-symmetric (across vertical meridian) areas, correlations were positive at 0–angular distance, and decreased at larger angular distances.
source: For comparisons between dorsal areas, between ventral areas, and between mirror-symmetric (across vertical meridian) areas, correlations were positive at 0–angular distance, and decreased at larger angular distances (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the angular distance analysis, with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: For within-quadrant, within-hemisphere and mirror symmetric (across vertical meridian) within-quadrant, between-hemisphere comparisons, correlations steadily decreased at larger angular distances.
source: For within-quadrant, within-hemisphere and mirror symmetric (across vertical meridian) within-quadrant, between-hemisphere comparisons, correlations steadily decreased at larger angular distances.
evidence: This is a finding from the angular distance analysis.

claim: These results suggest that angular connectivity reflects overlapping RF between areas and mirror-symmetric connections between hemispheres.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that angular connectivity reflects overlapping RF between areas and mirror-symmetric connections between hemispheres.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the angular distance findings.

claim: No effect of angular distance was observed between dorsal and ventral comparisons based on actual angular distance or when reflecting across the horizontal meridian (i.e., mirror symmetry).
source: No effect of angular distance was observed between dorsal and ventral comparisons based on actual angular distance or when reflecting across the horizontal meridian (i.e., mirror symmetry).
evidence: This is a negative finding from the angular distance analysis.

claim: For each area pair, the spatial pattern of correlations (across eccentricity bins) was similar between experimental conditions.
source: For each area pair, the spatial pattern of correlations (across eccentricity bins) was similar between experimental conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing correlation patterns across conditions.

claim: Across all areas, the average individual subject correlation of these spatial patterns between experimental conditions was 0.86 for intra-hemisphere comparisons and 0.75 for inter-hemisphere comparisons.
source: Across all areas, the average individual subject correlation of these spatial patterns between experimental conditions was 0.86 for intra-hemisphere comparisons and 0.75 for inter-hemisphere comparisons.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparing correlation patterns across conditions.

claim: The average individual subject correlation between resting-state and movie viewing conditions was 0.84 for intra-hemisphere comparisons and 0.71 for inter-hemisphere comparisons.
source: The average individual subject correlation between resting-state and movie viewing conditions was 0.84 for intra-hemisphere comparisons and 0.71 for inter-hemisphere comparisons.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from comparing resting and movie conditions.

claim: These data are consistent with the exploratory seed based analyses, and suggest that the spatial pattern of correlations between visual areas tested were similar in the presence and absence of a strong bottom-up input.
source: Overall, these data are consistent with the exploratory seed based analyses, and suggest that the spatial pattern of correlations between visual areas tested were similar in the presence and absence of a strong bottom-up input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings comparing conditions.

claim: This widespread eccentricity-based correlation pattern appears to reflect an eccentricity bias that is inherent to the organization of the visual system (i.e., stable during rest) and may support processing during active perception of the visual environment.
source: Given the similarity of correlation matrices across all three conditions, this widespread eccentricity-based correlation pattern appears to reflect an eccentricity bias that is inherent to the organization of the visual system (i.e., stable during rest) and may support processing during active perception of the visual environment (e.g., during movie viewing).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with speculation about functional significance.

claim: Intrinsic neural dynamics during the resting and movie conditions that are not related to the processing of visual stimuli, as well as non-neuronal artifacts, can only influence the pattern of correlations within each run, but should not induce correlations between runs.
source: Intrinsic neural dynamics during the resting and movie conditions that are not related to the processing of visual stimuli, as well as non-neuronal artifacts (e.g., respiratory rate, motion), can only influence the pattern of correlations within each run, but should not induce correlations between runs.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the nature of noise and artifact correlations.

claim: Inter-run Fisher-transformed correlations on resting state data showed no effect of radial distance (all ps > 0.05), validating the assumption that noise correlations should not be reliable across runs.
source: Indeed, inter-run Fisher-transformed correlations on resting state data showed no effect of radial distance (all ps > 0.05), validating the assumption that noise correlations should not be reliable across runs (Figure 7, blue and black lines).
evidence: This is a finding from the inter-run analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Inter-run correlations during movie watching showed radial distance effects similar to intra-run correlations.
source: In contrast, inter-run correlations during movie watching showed radial distance effects similar to intra-run correlations (Figure 7, red lines).
evidence: This is a finding from the inter-run analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Inter-run correlations were statistically significant for 96% of all comparisons (ps < 0.05, FDR corrected).
source: Inter-run correlations were statistically significant for 96% of all comparisons (ps < 0.05, FDR corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the inter-run analysis.

claim: The inter-run results indicate that the observed widespread eccentricity-based correlations can reflect the processing of the incoming information during viewing of real life stimuli.
source: The inter-run results indicate that the observed widespread eccentricity-based correlations can reflect the processing of the incoming information during viewing of real life stimuli, and further suggest that these correlations patterns are unlikely to be driven by non-neuronal artifacts.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the inter-run findings.

claim: The observed widespread eccentricity-based correlation pattern could not be attributed to non-neuronal artifacts (e.g., physiological noise, motion, BOLD spatial autocorrelation, eye movements).
source: We performed a variety of control analyses to rule out possible confounds. The observed widespread eccentricity-based correlation pattern could not be attributed to non-neuronal artifacts (e.g., physiological noise, motion, BOLD spatial autocorrelation, eye movements).
evidence: This is a conclusion from control analyses.

claim: Global artifacts did not drive our results as correlation patterns were strengthened by the removal of non-neuronal signals (i.e., motion and white matter).
source: Global artifacts did not drive our results as correlation patterns were strengthened by the removal of non-neuronal signals (i.e., motion and white matter).
evidence: This is a finding from control analyses.

claim: The eccentricity-based correlation pattern was not due to inherent spread of the BOLD signal, anatomical distance, or any biases in our analyses, as artificial data that preserved such biases were not correlated with radial distance.
source: The eccentricity-based correlation pattern was not due to inherent spread of the BOLD signal, anatomical distance, or any biases in our analyses, as artificial data that preserved such biases were not correlated with radial distance (see Box 2; Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion from control analyses using artificial data, with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: Subject motion also could not explain the observed correlation patterns.
source: Subject motion also could not explain the observed correlation patterns.
evidence: This is a conclusion from control analyses.

claim: The strength of eccentricity correlation did not significantly co-vary with degree of subject movement.
source: Further, the strength of eccentricity correlation did not significantly co-vary with degree of subject movement.
evidence: This is a finding from correlation analysis between motion and effect strength.

claim: There was no significant correlation across subjects between the mean slope (averaged across all area pairs) and any of the six motion parameters (all rs < 0.24, ps > 0.05).
source: We performed Spearman rank correlations between each subject's total amount of movement and the slope of his or her radial bin distance coefficients (i.e., effect of eccentricity on correlation strength). There was no significant correlation across subjects between the mean slope (averaged across all area pairs) and any of the six motion parameters (all rs < 0.24, ps > 0.05).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the motion control analysis.

claim: There were no significant correlations across subjects between the slope and total amount of movement for any individual area pair (ps > 0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: In addition, there were no significant correlations across subjects between the slope and total amount of movement for any individual area pair (ps > 0.05, FDR-corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the motion control analysis.

claim: It is unlikely that eye movements drove the eccentricity-based correlation pattern as similar results were observed at rest during both fixation and eyes closed conditions.
source: It is unlikely that eye movements drove the eccentricity-based correlation pattern as similar results were observed at rest during both fixation and eyes closed conditions.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing conditions with different eye movement possibilities.

claim: Significant inter-run eccentricity-based correlation patterns were observed during movie viewing, but not during rest, further ruling out the possible influence of non-neuronal intrinsic artifacts.
source: Finally, significant inter-run eccentricity-based correlation patterns were observed during movie viewing, but not during rest, further ruling out the possible influence of non-neuronal intrinsic artifacts (e.g., respiration rate, cardiac rate, motion), which should not be correlated across runs.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the inter-run analysis.

claim: Both local and widespread connectivity patterns contributed to the spatial pattern of observed correlations.
source: Both local and widespread connectivity patterns contributed to the spatial pattern of observed correlations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the topographic model regression analysis.

claim: Correlations were qualitatively strongest at the intersection of iso-polar angle and iso-eccentricity, and were generally elevated along iso-eccentricity representations, irrespective of polar angle distance.
source: Correlations were qualitatively strongest at the intersection of iso-polar angle and iso-eccentricity, and were generally elevated along iso-eccentricity representations, irrespective of polar angle distance (Figure 8).
evidence: This is a finding from the topographic model analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The strongest overlapping RF effects were observed for intra-areal comparisons whereas eccentricity effects were consistently observed across all comparisons and were much larger than overlapping RF and polar angle effects for inter-hemisphere comparisons.
source: In general, the strongest overlapping RF effects were observed for intra-areal comparisons whereas eccentricity effects were consistently observed across all comparisons and were much larger than overlapping RF and polar angle effects for inter-hemisphere comparisons.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the topographic model regression analysis.

claim: The combination of local and widespread predictors well fit intra-area correlation patterns, and moderately fit inter-area and inter-hemisphere patterns.
source: For individual subjects, the combination of local and widespread predictors well fit intra-area correlation patterns, and moderately fit inter-area and inter-hemisphere patterns.
evidence: This is a finding from the full model regression analysis.

claim: The average individual subject variance explained by the full model ranged between 40% and 68% for intra-areal comparisons and between 11% and 28% for inter-areal comparisons.
source: The average individual subject variance explained by the full model ranged between 40% and 68% for intra-areal comparisons and between 11% and 28% for inter-areal comparisons.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the full model regression analysis.

claim: Across subjects, the coefficients for the overlapping RF predictor were significantly positive for all intra-hemisphere, intra-areal comparisons as well as for most other comparisons (ps < 0.05, FDR-corrected).
source: Across subjects, the coefficients for the overlapping RF predictor were significantly positive for all intra-hemisphere, intra-areal comparisons as well as for most other comparisons (ps < 0.05, FDR-corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the full model regression analysis.

claim: Coefficients for the eccentricity predictor were significantly positive for all but one comparison (V1–hV4 inter-hemisphere) (ps < 0.05, FDR corrected).
source: Coefficients for the eccentricity predictor were significantly positive for all but one comparison (V1–hV4 inter-hemisphere) (ps < 0.05, FDR corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the full model regression analysis.

claim: Coefficients for the polar angle predictor were significantly positive for most intra-hemisphere comparisons, but only for a few inter-hemisphere comparisons (ps < 0.05, FDR corrected).
source: Coefficients for the polar angle predictor were significantly positive for most intra-hemisphere comparisons, but only for a few inter-hemisphere comparisons (ps < 0.05, FDR corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the full model regression analysis.

claim: Both eccentricity and polar angle predictors were strongly correlated with the overlapping RF predictor for most intra-hemisphere area pairs (mean r = 0.54; STD = 0.08).
source: Though these results suggest some effect of both local and widespread connectivity, we found that both eccentricity and polar angle predictors were strongly correlated with the overlapping RF predictor for most intra-hemisphere area pairs (mean r = 0.54; STD = 0.08).
evidence: This is a finding about collinearity between predictors.

claim: Since the local and widespread predictors have a non-trivial degree of collinearity, the coefficient estimates for individual predictors from the full model may not be accurate for intra-hemisphere comparisons.
source: Since the local and widespread predictors have a non-trivial degree of collinearity, the coefficient estimates for individual predictors from the full model may not be accurate for intra-hemisphere comparisons, which had the strongest correlations between local and widespread predictors.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of the full model analysis.

claim: It is very unlikely that all of the widespread effects can generically be explained by the overlapping receptive field model since significant correlations were observed in the eccentricity bin analyses between iso-eccentricity representations in distinct parts of visual space.
source: However, it is very unlikely that all of the widespread effects can generically be explained by the overlapping receptive field model since significant correlations were observed in the eccentricity bin analyses between iso-eccentricity representations in distinct parts of visual space (Figure 6; e.g., between V2d RH and V2v LH).
evidence: This is an inference from the eccentricity bin analysis results, with reference to a figure.

claim: When removing the shared variance between local and widespread connectivity predictors, significant effects of eccentricity connectivity were still observed.
source: When removing the shared variance between local and widespread connectivity predictors, significant effects of eccentricity connectivity were still observed.
evidence: This is a finding from the residual correlation analysis.

claim: The average correlation coefficient between the residual pattern and the eccentricity predictor was similar across most areas for both within and across hemispheres.
source: The average correlation coefficient between the residual pattern and the eccentricity predictor was similar across most areas for both within and across hemispheres (Figure 9, medium gray bars).
evidence: This is a finding from the residual correlation analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The Fisher-transformed individual subject eccentricity residual correlations were reliably different from zero for 56/60 visual area pairs across rest and movie viewing experiments (ps < 0.05, FDR corrected).
source: The Fisher-transformed individual subject eccentricity residual correlations were reliably different from zero for 56/60 visual area pairs across rest and movie viewing experiments (ps < 0.05, FDR corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the residual correlation analysis.

claim: Residual correlations that included hV4 were weaker than residual correlations between areas V1, V2, and V3.
source: Consistent with the binning analyses, residual correlations that included hV4 were weaker than residual correlations between areas V1, V2, and V3.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing residual correlations across areas.

claim: There was no clear, consistent effect of the polar angle predictor across areas.
source: In contrast, there was no clear, consistent effect of the polar angle predictor across areas (Figure 9, lightest gray bars).
evidence: This is a finding from the residual correlation analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: The polar angle residual correlations were only significantly positive for 4/60 pairs (ps < 0.05, FDR corrected).
source: The polar angle residual correlations were only significantly positive for 4/60 pairs (ps < 0.05, FDR corrected).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the residual correlation analysis.

claim: The residual pattern was more correlated with the eccentricity predictor than with the polar angle predictor for 49/60 pairs (ps < 0.05, FDR corrected).
source: The residual pattern was more correlated with the eccentricity predictor than with the polar angle predictor for 49/60 pairs (ps < 0.05, FDR corrected) (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the residual correlation analysis, with reference to a figure.

claim: Widespread eccentricity-based connectivity effects were consistently observed before and after removal of local connectivity variance.
source: Widespread eccentricity-based connectivity effects were consistently observed before and after removal of local connectivity variance.
evidence: This is a summary finding from the model analyses.

claim: Even when attributing all shared variance between local and widespread predictors to the local predictor, eccentricity-based effects were still observed.
source: Even when attributing all shared variance between local and widespread predictors to the local predictor, eccentricity-based effects were still observed.
evidence: This is a finding from the conservative residual analysis approach.

claim: Consistent polar angle effects were generally only observed prior to removal of local connectivity variance.
source: In contrast, consistent polar angle effects were generally only observed prior to removal of local connectivity variance.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing full model and residual analyses.

claim: Eccentricity effects were generally stronger than polar angle both before and after removal of local connectivity variance, suggesting that this difference is driven by asymmetries in widespread, not local, connectivity patterns.
source: Eccentricity effects were generally stronger than polar angle both before and after removal of local connectivity variance, suggesting that this difference is driven by asymmetries in widespread, not local, connectivity patterns.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the comparative findings.

claim: The variance explained by the local connectivity model was strongly correlated with both eccentricity (mean r across areas = 0.50; STD = 0.08) and polar angle (mean r across areas = 0.49; STD = 0.07) predictors, and there was little difference between them (mean r difference across areas = 0.01; STD = 0.06).
source: In further support of this, the variance explained by the local connectivity model was strongly correlated with both eccentricity (mean r across areas = 0.50; STD = 0.08) and polar angle (mean r across areas = 0.49; STD = 0.07) predictors, and there was little difference between them (mean r difference across areas = 0.01; STD = 0.06).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding about the relationship between local and widespread predictors.

claim: These data suggest that connectivity effects based on overlapping RFs are comparable along eccentricity and polar angle axes (i.e., isotropic with respect to visual field), which is consistent with anatomical studies in macaques that suggest visual field coverage of local, lateral connections is generally isotropic.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that connectivity effects based on overlapping RFs are comparable along eccentricity and polar angle axes (i.e., isotropic with respect to visual field), which is consistent with anatomical studies in macaques that suggest visual field coverage of local, lateral connections is generally isotropic (Angelucci et al., 2002).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings with support from cited anatomical studies.

claim: The pattern of widespread correlated BOLD signal beyond overlapping receptive fields reflects eccentricity organization.
source: Importantly, the pattern of widespread correlated BOLD signal beyond overlapping receptive fields reflects eccentricity organization.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the study.

claim: For inter-hemisphere comparisons, the homotopic RF predictor generally captured more variance than the overlapping RF predictor.
source: Indeed, for inter-hemisphere comparisons, the homotopic RF predictor generally captured more variance than the overlapping RF predictor.
evidence: This is a finding from the homotopic connectivity analysis.

claim: The eccentricity effects were still present in residual correlations after removing all variance explained by the homotopic RF predictor.
source: We removed all variance explained by the homotopic RF predictor then recomputed the residual correlations. The eccentricity effects were still present in these residual correlations (Figure 9—figure supplement 3), though intra-areal hV4 correlations were notably weaker.
evidence: This is a finding from the homotopic connectivity control analysis, with reference to a figure supplement.

claim: The eccentricity-based connectivity effects were not driven by homotopic RF connectivity.
source: Overall, these data show that the eccentricity-based connectivity effects were not driven by homotopic RF connectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the homotopic connectivity control analysis.

claim: The variance explained by the overlapping RF model (after accounting for patterns attributable to the 'noise' model) was generally greater than the variance explained by the model of residual widespread connectivity (after removal of overlapping RF connectivity effects) for within hemisphere comparisons (mean ratio across areas, conditions = 1.69:1.00).
source: The variance explained by the overlapping RF model (after accounting for patterns attributable to the 'noise' model) was generally greater than the variance explained by the model of residual widespread connectivity (after removal of overlapping RF connectivity effects) for within hemisphere comparisons (mean ratio across areas, conditions = 1.69:1.00).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model contributions.

claim: For between hemisphere comparisons, variance explained by the overlapping RF model was weaker than the variance explained by the model of residual widespread connectivity without accounting for mirror symmetrical connections (mean ratio across areas, condition = 1.00:5.65), but was generally greater when accounting for these connections (mean ratio across areas, condition = 1.27:1.00).
source: For between hemisphere comparisons, variance explained by the overlapping RF model (after accounting for patterns attributable to the 'noise' model) was weaker than the variance explained by the model of residual widespread connectivity without accounting for mirror symmetrical connections (mean ratio across areas, condition = 1.00:5.65), but was generally greater when accounting for these connections (mean ratio across areas, condition = 1.27:1.00).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of model contributions for inter-hemisphere comparisons.

claim: Both topographically local and widespread connectivity patterns significantly contributed to the observed correlation patterns across V1, V2, V3 and hV4.
source: In summary, these data demonstrate that both topographically local and widespread connectivity patterns significantly contributed to the observed correlation patterns across V1, V2, V3 and hV4.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the topographic model analyses.

claim: The eccentricity correlation patterns explained an additional, significant amount of variance in our data, which was not accounted for by the local connectivity model.
source: Critically, the eccentricity correlation patterns explained an additional, significant amount of variance in our data, which was not accounted for by the local connectivity model.
evidence: This is a key conclusion from the model analyses.

claim: For most inter-hemispheric comparisons, adding the eccentricity predictor more than doubled the variance explained by the local connectivity model, suggesting that it was the major component of the correlation patterns between hemispheres.
source: For most inter-hemispheric comparisons, adding the eccentricity predictor more than doubled the variance explained by the local connectivity model, suggesting that it was the major component of the correlation patterns between hemispheres.
evidence: This is a finding about the relative importance of eccentricity for inter-hemispheric correlations.

claim: After accounting for overlapping pRF connectivity, the strength of eccentricity correlations were similar within and across hemispheres for most comparisons between V1, V2, and V3, suggesting that this widespread connectivity pattern uniformly spans the whole visual field.
source: Notably, after accounting for overlapping pRF connectivity, the strength of eccentricity correlations were similar within and across hemispheres for most comparisons between V1, V2, and V3, suggesting that this widespread connectivity pattern uniformly spans the whole visual field.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the residual correlation findings.

claim: Our data extend recent findings of topographic connectivity within visual cortex using fMRI.
source: Our data extend recent findings of topographic connectivity within visual cortex using fMRI.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the study to the literature.

claim: At a fine-scale, correlation patterns reflect overlapping RFs within hemispheres and homotopic connections between hemispheres.
source: At a fine-scale, correlation patterns reflect overlapping RFs within hemispheres and homotopic connections between hemispheres (Heinzle et al., 2011; Haak et al., 2012; Butt et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of prior findings supported by citations.

claim: By modeling V1 inter-areal connections based on overlapping RFs, Gravel and colleagues (2014) generated polar angle and eccentricity maps for V2 and V3.
source: By modeling V1 inter-areal connections based on overlapping RFs, Gravel and colleagues (2014) generated polar angle and eccentricity maps for V2 and V3.
evidence: This is a summary of a prior study supported by citation.

claim: Raemaekers and colleagues (2014) reported that fine-scaled connectivity was only observable after filtering coarse-scale components.
source: However, Raemaekers and colleagues (2014) reported that such fine-scaled connectivity was only observable after filtering coarse-scale components.
evidence: This is a summary of a prior study supported by citation.

claim: At a coarse scale, there has been evidence for a general foveal-peripheral distinction.
source: At a coarse scale, there has been evidence for a general foveal-peripheral distinction (Vincent et al., 2007; Nallasamy and Tsao, 2011; Smith et al., 2012; Raemaekers et al., 2014), but these studies did not report a systematic topography of correlation patterns that reflects the underlying eccentricity organization, nor were effects of overlapping RFs and cortical distance controlled.
evidence: This is a summary of prior findings with citations, noting limitations of those studies.

claim: Evidence for a more systematic relation to eccentricity was reported between V1 and ventral V3, though such data are also consistent with overlapping RF connectivity as well as cortical distance since only ventral V3 was probed.
source: Evidence for a more systematic relation to eccentricity was reported between V1 and ventral V3 (Yeo et al., 2011), though such data are also consistent with overlapping RF connectivity as well as cortical distance since only ventral V3 was probed.
evidence: This is a summary of a prior study with citation, noting alternative interpretations.

claim: We explicitly and quantitatively combined these connectivity phenomena in a fine-grained analysis across a wider range of brain regions, replicating previous findings of overlapping RF and homotopic correlation patterns without filtering coarse spatial components.
source: Here, we explicitly and quantitatively combined these connectivity phenomena in a fine-grained analysis across a wider range of brain regions, replicating previous findings of overlapping RF and homotopic correlation patterns without filtering coarse spatial components (Heinzle et al., 2011; Haak et al., 2012; Butt et al., 2013; Gravel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the study's approach and contribution, with citations to prior work.

claim: Even after accounting for these patterns, we found a robust widespread correlation pattern that reflects the eccentricity organization across much of visual cortex.
source: Even after accounting for these patterns, we found a robust widespread correlation pattern that reflects the eccentricity organization across much of visual cortex.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study.

claim: Such systematic correlation patterns suggest orderly integration processes across the whole visual field at multiple levels of the processing hierarchy, not just a foveal-peripheral dichotomy.
source: Such systematic correlation patterns suggest orderly integration processes across the whole visual field at multiple levels of the processing hierarchy, not just a foveal-peripheral dichotomy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings about functional significance.

claim: Eccentricity-based correlation patterns may reflect an intrinsic functional organization of visual cortex.
source: Eccentricity-based correlation patterns may reflect an intrinsic functional organization of visual cortex.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Our results during rest demonstrate that regions with iso-eccentricity representations are likely to be co-active, even in the absence of visual input.
source: Our results during rest demonstrate that regions with iso-eccentricity representations are likely to be co-active, even in the absence of visual input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the resting state findings.

claim: Our results during the movie viewing condition demonstrate that the temporal dynamics yielding these eccentricity-based correlation patterns are also present during strong bottom-up input, and indicate that this organization is relevant for the processing of incoming visual input.
source: Our results during the movie viewing condition demonstrate that the temporal dynamics yielding these eccentricity-based correlation patterns are also present during strong bottom-up input, and indicate that this organization is relevant for the processing of incoming visual input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the movie viewing findings.

claim: Studies in macaques and cats have shown that the activity of neurons with similar response properties are correlated in the presence and absence of external input, suggesting that spontaneous neuronal activity is tightly linked to intrinsic cortical networks.
source: In agreement with these findings, studies in macaques and cats have shown that the activity of neurons with similar response properties are correlated in the presence and absence of external input, suggesting that spontaneous neuronal activity is tightly linked to intrinsic cortical networks (Arieli et al., 1995; Tsodyks et al., 1999; Goldberg et al., 2004; Ghuman et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a summary of prior findings with citations, used to support the interpretation.

claim: Both overlapping RF and eccentricity-based connectivity patterns were observed in the presence and absence of external input, suggesting that topographically-local and widespread patterns are both part of this intrinsic functional architecture.
source: Further, both overlapping RF and eccentricity-based connectivity patterns were observed in the presence and absence of external input, suggesting that topographically-local and widespread patterns are both part of this intrinsic functional architecture.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings across conditions.

claim: The observed patterns of functional connectivity may reflect both direct and indirect anatomical connectivity.
source: The observed patterns of functional connectivity may reflect both direct and indirect anatomical connectivity (Vincent et al., 2007; Honey et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with support from citations.

claim: Local connectivity is likely supported by direct anatomical connections between overlapping RFs.
source: Local connectivity is likely supported by direct anatomical connections between overlapping RFs (Cragg, 1969; Essen and Zeki, 1978; Maunsell and Van Essen, 1983).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Such wiring is necessary for the integration of information within focal points of our visual environment.
source: Such wiring is necessary for the integration of information within focal points of our visual environment.
evidence: This is an inference about functional significance based on anatomical knowledge.

claim: Direct intra-areal anatomical connections between dorsal and ventral visual cortex at the horizontal meridians and between both hemispheres at the vertical meridians could support widespread functional connectivity across the visual field.
source: Direct intra-areal anatomical connections between dorsal and ventral visual cortex at the horizontal meridians (Jeffs et al., 2009) and between both hemispheres at the vertical meridians (Hubel and Wiesel, 1967; Essen and Zeki, 1978; Newsome and Allman, 1980; Cusick et al., 1984; Kennedy et al., 1986) could support widespread functional connectivity across the visual field, though we are not aware of anatomical studies explicitly reporting eccentricity-based patterns of intra-areal connectivity.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with support from citations, noting a gap in the literature.

claim: While labeled cells of lateral connections in macaque striate and extrastriate cortex exhibit some anisotropy with respect to the cortical surface, this is thought to reflect cortical magnification factor, and yield isotropic visual field coverage.
source: Further, while labeled cells of lateral connections in macaque striate and extrastriate cortex exhibit some anisotropy with respect to the cortical surface, this is thought to reflect cortical magnification factor, and yield isotropic visual field coverage (Angelucci et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a summary of prior anatomical findings with citation.

claim: Consistent with the anatomical connectivity, we found that correlation patterns between regions with overlapping RFs were comparable along eccentricity and polar angle dimensions.
source: Consistent with the anatomical connectivity, we found that correlation patterns between regions with overlapping RFs were comparable along eccentricity and polar angle dimensions.
evidence: This is a finding that is consistent with anatomical knowledge.

claim: Beyond overlapping RFs, correlation patterns were anisotropic (with respect to visual field coverage) and reflected the underlying eccentricity organization.
source: Beyond overlapping RFs, correlation patterns were anisotropic (with respect to visual field coverage) and reflected the underlying eccentricity organization.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study.

claim: The observed eccentricity-based correlation patterns may actually reflect a broader-scale anatomical organization of direct (and indirect) connections, facilitated via differences in intra-areal projections between cortical sites representing central and peripheral space.
source: Alternatively, the observed eccentricity-based correlation patterns may actually reflect a broader-scale anatomical organization of direct (and indirect) connections, facilitated via differences in intra-areal projections between cortical sites representing central and peripheral space (Colby et al., 1988; Nakamura et al., 1993; Gattass et al., 2005; Ungerleider et al., 2008, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with support from citations.

claim: Such a distinction has been characterized in the patterns of supra-areal anatomical connections between early visual and extrastriate cortex in non-human primates.
source: Such a distinction has been characterized in the patterns of supra-areal anatomical connections between early visual and extrastriate cortex in non-human primates (Rosa, 2002; Gattass et al., 2005; Rosa and Tweedale, 2005; Rosa et al., 2009; Buckner and Yeo, 2014).
evidence: This is a summary of prior anatomical findings with citations.

claim: It is not known whether these anatomical connectivity patterns are 'bi-modal', and only distinguish central and peripheral space, or reflect a finer-scale organization where connectivity patterns with intermediate eccentricity representations are distinguishable from central and peripheral connectivity profiles.
source: It is not known whether these anatomical connectivity patterns are 'bi-modal', and only distinguish central and peripheral space, or reflect a finer-scale organization where connectivity patterns with intermediate eccentricity representations are distinguishable from central and peripheral connectivity profiles.
evidence: This is a statement about a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Our results predict that these anatomical connections should reflect a gradient, though this remains to be explored.
source: Our results predict that these anatomical connections should reflect a gradient, though this remains to be explored.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the study's findings.

claim: Feedback projections from extrastriate areas with receptive fields covering wide swaths of the visual field to early and intermediate visual areas could facilitate such widespread, eccentricity-dependent correlation patterns.
source: In particular, feedback projections from extrastriate areas with receptive fields covering wide swaths of the visual field to early and intermediate visual areas could facilitate such widespread, eccentricity-dependent correlation patterns.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism to explain the findings.

claim: When comparing the profile of anatomical connectivity between V2/V4 and higher order cortex with the organization of eccentricity across visual cortex in macaques, it is clear that higher order areas connected with peripheral parts of V2 and V4 have a large representation of the periphery, and higher order areas connected with foveal parts of V2 and V4 have a large representation of the fovea.
source: It is interesting to note that when comparing the profile of anatomical connectivity between V2/V4 and higher order cortex (e.g., Figure 7, Gattass et al., 2005) with the organization of eccentricity across visual cortex in macaques (Brewer et al., 2002; Kolster et al., 2009; Arcaro et al., 2011), it is clear that higher order areas connected with peripheral parts of V2 and V4 (e.g., PO, PIP, LIP, DP, TF) have a large representation of the periphery, and higher order areas connected with foveal parts of V2 and V4 (e.g., TEO and TE) have a large representation of the fovea.
evidence: This is an observation from comparing prior anatomical and functional mapping studies, supported by citations.

claim: The exact relationship between the observed correlation patterns and anatomical pathways will need to be further investigated.
source: The exact relationship between the observed correlation patterns and anatomical pathways will need to be further investigated.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: Our data link the functional organization of early and higher order visual cortex.
source: Our data link the functional organization of early and higher order visual cortex.
evidence: This is a statement about the contribution of the study.

claim: Previous studies have proposed eccentricity as a large-scale functional organizing principle for higher order visual cortex.
source: Previous studies have proposed eccentricity as a large-scale functional organizing principle for higher order visual cortex (Levy et al., 2001; Hasson et al., 2002; Malach et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a summary of prior theoretical work with citations.

claim: Higher order areas with foveal biases tend to be specialized in face and object recognition, and areas with peripheral biases tend to be involved in scene analysis.
source: Higher order areas with foveal biases tend to be specialized in face and object recognition, and areas with peripheral biases tend to be involved in scene analysis (Levy et al., 2001; Hasson et al., 2002; Malach et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a summary of prior findings with citations.

claim: These recognition processes require different visual acuities.
source: Perceptually, these recognition processes require different visual acuities.
evidence: This is a statement based on perceptual knowledge.

claim: Fine acuity is needed for the featural discrimination among similar face and object exemplars.
source: For example, while fine acuity is needed for the featural discrimination among similar face and object exemplars (Fiorentini et al., 1983; Goffaux et al., 2005; Keil, 2008), a coarser acuity is needed for mapping the surrounding layout necessary for navigation in space (Oliva and Schyns, 1997; Oliva and Torralba, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about perceptual requirements supported by citations.

claim: A coarser acuity is needed for mapping the surrounding layout necessary for navigation in space.
source: For example, while fine acuity is needed for the featural discrimination among similar face and object exemplars (Fiorentini et al., 1983; Goffaux et al., 2005; Keil, 2008), a coarser acuity is needed for mapping the surrounding layout necessary for navigation in space (Oliva and Schyns, 1997; Oliva and Torralba, 2006).
evidence: This is a statement about perceptual requirements supported by citations.

claim: Eye movement patterns during scene perception are related to the types of information within a scene.
source: Further, eye movement patterns during scene perception are related to the types of information within a scene (Buswell, 1935; Henderson and Hollingworth, 1999).
evidence: This is a summary of prior findings with citations.

claim: People tend to foveate on faces while orienting their peripheral vision at landscape features and room contours.
source: People tend to foveate on faces while orienting their peripheral vision at landscape features and room contours (Yarbus, 1967).
evidence: This is a summary of a prior finding with citation.

claim: These eccentricity biases are also reflected in the connectivity patterns between face and place category-selective regions in ventral temporal cortex with extrastriate visual area hV4.
source: These eccentricity biases are also reflected in the connectivity patterns between face and place category-selective regions in ventral temporal cortex with extrastriate visual area hV4 (Baldassano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a summary of a prior finding with citation.

claim: Our data show that this divergence in the computational processes necessary for foveal and peripheral recognition is evident even in early visual cortex.
source: Our data show that this divergence in the computational processes necessary for foveal and peripheral recognition is evident even in early visual cortex.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings in the context of prior work.

claim: Our results underscore the importance of relating functional connectivity data to known functional (or anatomical) organization.
source: Our results underscore the importance of relating functional connectivity data to known functional (or anatomical) organization (Jbabdi et al., 2013; Sporns and Honey, 2013; Wang et al., 2013).

source: The detailed retinotopic organization of visual cortex allowed for a unique opportunity to systematically compare patterns of correlated BOLD activity with the known underlying functional organization of the visual system.

source: Across subjects and experiments, correlations were stronger between areas at matched eccentricities than within areas at large eccentricity distances, suggesting that functional connectivity analyses on BOLD data are more sensitive at revealing widespread, inter-areal connectivity patterns than the localization of individual retinotopic areas (see also Yeo et al., 2011).

claim: We propose that relating correlation patterns to known functional and anatomical data will prove important for identifying the functional pathways for the integration of information across individual, functionally specialized areas.
